bib.title: MedBrowseComp: Benchmarking Medical Deep Research and Computer Use

legacy_report:
SOURCE: "MedBrowseComp: Benchmarking Medical Deep Research and Computer Use". First author Shan Chen (co-first with Pedro Moreira). Affiliations: Harvard, Mass General Brigham, Boston Children's Hospital, MIT, Universitat Pompeu Fabra, Johns Hopkins, Brown, HemOnc.org, Maastricht, UVA. Corresponding author Danielle S. Bitterman. arXiv:2505.14963v1 [cs.CL], 20 May 2025. Venue: preprint ("Preprint. Under review." p.1). The PDF carries a NeurIPS checklist.

COVERAGE: All 26 pages were extracted (77,174 chars). Pages 1-21 were read closely: main text, tables, limitations, appendices A.1-A.5. Pages 22-26 are the NeurIPS checklist boilerplate and were skimmed. The extraction was clean, and the judge-prompt appendix A.2/A.3 text is verbatim code or prompt. There were no embedded instructions, though the A.3 system prompt for the computer-use agent contains instruction-like text, which is data.

CORE CLAIM: A benchmark of 1,000+ multi-hop medical fact-seeking questions, built from HemOnc.org linked to PubMed, ClinicalTrials.gov, the FDA Orange Book and Yahoo Finance. Accuracy falls monotonically as hop count rises. Agents that browse iteratively beat single-shot search. GUI computer-use agents do worse than API-driven deep research.

HEADLINE NUMBERS
1. MedBrowseComp-50 (n=50, 10 per hop depth 1-5). One run per system, judged by GPT-4.1 mini plus human check. Table 5 (p.17):
   - O3 deep research: 25.5/50 (51.0%). O3 search: 19/50 (38.0%).
   - Gemini 2.5 Pro deep search: 24.5/50 (49.0%). Gemini 2.5 Pro search: 14/50 (28.0%).
   - Perplexity deep research: 20/50 (40.0%). Sonar Pro: 10/50 (20.0%).
   - Claude 3.7 Sonnet computer use: 18/50 (36.0%).
   - Best-of-1-among-all (post hoc oracle across systems): 30/50.
   - Half credit was given on one 2-hop question where the model returned the company name instead of the sub-entity.
2. Hop decay, MedBrowseComp-50, 5-hop (n=10): O3 deep research 1/10, Gemini deep search 0/10, Perplexity deep research 0/10, Sonar Pro 0/10 (all per Table 5). Computer use scored 1/10 at 5 hops.
3. MedBrowseComp-605 (n=605 = 121 per hop, one run, LLM judge only, Table 6 p.18):
   - Gemini 2.5 Pro search: 182/605 (30.1%) against 80/605 (13.2%) for the parametric-only model.
   - Sonar Pro: 158/605 (26.1%).
   - GPT-4.1: 80/605 (13.2%) with search against 105/605 (17.3%) parametric-only. Search is worse.
   - Gemini 2 Flash: 138/605 (22.8%) with search against 113/605 (18.7%) parametric-only.
   - Strict "REAL accuracy" excludes questions whose correct answer is "not applicable" (n=453, Table 7). Gemini 2.5 Pro search scores 111/453 (24.5%); GPT-4.1 search 25/453 (5.5%).
   - On REAL 4-hop (n=39), Gemini 2.5 Pro search scores 2/39 (5.1%) and 5-hop (n=51) 0/51. The other REAL cells at 4 and 5 hops are 0 except Sonar Pro 1/51 and Gemini 2 Flash 1/51 at 5 hops.
   - Many raw 4-hop scores in Table 6 look inflated by "not applicable" answers: GPT-4.1 param is 60/121 (49.6%) raw but 0/39 REAL.
4. Computer-use diagnostic (Claude 3.7 Sonnet, 121 questions per task, p.8 Table 2): trial ID 33.88%, start date 30.58%, second author 36.36%, PMID 11.57%. Starting from the HemOnc.org homepage (Table 8, p.19): PMID 42.98%, second author 46.28%, NCT 39.67%, start date 31.40%.
5. Judge reliability: two annotators answered MedBrowseComp-50 with "100% inter-annotator agreements and 98% agreement with GPT 4.1 mini" (p.5). Total experiment cost was $3,690, about $2,500 of it for computer use (p.9).

QUOTES
- "legacy leaderboards track static knowledge recall, whereas agentic systems should plan, browse, and synthesize fresh evidence in real time." (p.1)
- "by the 4- and 5-hop levels, RAG provides virtually no additional benefit over the bare model." (p.7)
- Context cost: "Every GUI action produces roughly two screenshots, inflating the context window to ∼ 200,000 tokens—compared with only ∼ 2,000 tokens for an equivalent text-only workflow." (p.9)

Trajectory error taxonomy, which suits an agent-eval note:
- Deep research (Table 1, p.7): inefficient tool allocation, poor source selection, unable to parse long tables.
- Computer use (Table 3, p.8): greedy attribute extraction, overlooking information, aimless wandering.

LIMITS
- No numbers are repeated: each system ran once, so there are no k-run variances or confidence intervals. The 50-question subset gives 10 questions per hop, and one question moves a score by 2 points.
- MedBrowseComp-50 was graded by LLM and human, while MedBrowseComp-605 was graded by LLM only ("lightly-audited").
- The comparison is confounded. Subscription products (O3 on Pro, Gemini on One) were queried by hand on different dates (28 Apr to 6 May 2025), and the systems differ in tools, not just models.
- Computer use covered only four 1-2-hop task types, so it is not comparable across the same hop depths.
- Operator, Mariner and UI-TARS were not tested. No clinicians reviewed the answers. Coverage is oncology and hematology only. The questions are "contamination-encoded" in the released set.
- The conclusion says "no system... exceeds 40% accuracy among questions that require more than a single hop" and "nearly half as many questions as their deep research counterparts". These do not obviously match the tables.
- Internal inconsistencies:
  - The abstract says "as low as 10%", the introduction says "<50% overall".
  - Table 8 refers to "Table 4" but means Table 2.
  - The 4-hop raw scores are inflated by NA-like answers.
- The "30%/4%" and "67%/7.4%" RAG boost figures on p.7 are unclear in the extraction. Do not cite them.
- Dated: tested May 2025 systems.

BUILDS ON: BrowseComp (Wei et al. 2025, arXiv 2504.12516), the explicit design inspiration. Also GAIA, WebWalker, FRAMES, SimpleQA, Humanity's Last Exam (judge prompt adapted), BrowseComp-ZH, Anthropic's computer-use demo codebase, and the HemOnc Dataverse (Warner et al. 2019).

BEST-FIT SECTION: Place it in 06-evaluating-agents.md under "Agent-specific suites" (line 364). It fits there as a domain-specific BrowseComp-style suite, and the hop-depth breakdown and the trajectory failure modes are relevant to "Scoring tool calls". A secondary fit is the REAL-accuracy point (excluding NA answers) under "Efficiency metrics" or "Pitfalls". 03-eval-datasets.md#lessons-from-public-benchmarks is a reasonable alternative only for the saturation argument, which is the "static benchmarks are saturated" opening. For the agent evaluation content, 06 is the better fit.

FIGURE: Figure 3 (p.6), overall performance by system with cost on the x-axis and the best-of-1-among-all aggregate. Table 5 (p.17) shows the hop-decay pattern more precisely. Figure 1 (p.3) has example multi-hop question constructions.

PROBLEMS: None in extraction. The Figure 3 content is a chart and was not rendered, so I read its caption only.
